set.stem: A 22-year-old man has a 2-cm thyroid nodule. His family history includes thyroid carcinoma and an unknown abdominal tumour in his father, now deceased; his BP is 145/90 mmHg. Fine-needle aspiration shows medullary thyroid carcinoma. Screening for which of the following must be undertaken before treatment of the thyroid carcinoma?
set.explanation: Familial medullary carcinoma suggests MEN2: exclude phaeochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) first, as an unrecognised tumour can cause a fatal crisis at thyroidectomy.
In differentiated thyroid cancer, age is the strongest prognostic factor (AJCC 8th: ≥55 years is high risk); a 1-cm node-negative tumour otherwise has an excellent outlook.
Graves disease with severe ophthalmopathy is best treated surgically (now usually total thyroidectomy); radioiodine can worsen the eye disease and drugs alone often relapse.
Catecholamine excess is confirmed biochemically first (plasma free or 24-h urinary metanephrines; here 24-h urinary VMA/noradrenaline), then the tumour is localised by CT/MRI.

set.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer (including a sister with a deleterious BRCA1 mutation) is found to carry the same mutation. Which range represents the lifetime risk of breast cancer that should be quoted to her?
set.explanation: BRCA1 carriers have a lifetime breast cancer risk of about 60–70% (quoted as 50–80%), with a high risk of ovarian cancer too.

set.stem: For the same patient with a BRCA1 mutation, which of the following management strategies is an accepted option for her high-risk status?
set.explanation: Options for BRCA carriers are annual MRI (± mammography) surveillance, chemoprevention (tamoxifen) and bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy ± salpingo-oophorectomy; unilateral mastectomy is not enough.

set.stem: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with a unifocal 2.5-cm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast with a clinically and sonographically normal axilla. Following MDT discussion, which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
set.explanation: A unifocal tumour suitable for breast conservation with a negative axilla: wide local excision with sentinel node biopsy, then radiotherapy and systemic therapy by histology.
Inflammatory breast cancer (dermal lymphatic invasion) is treated with trimodality therapy: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, modified radical mastectomy, then radiotherapy.
Standard regimens are anthracycline–cyclophosphamide followed by a taxane, with trastuzumab/pertuzumab added for HER2-positive disease (e.g. TCHP).
The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women aged 50 to 70 (up to their 71st birthday) for mammography every 3 years.
A 4-cm node-negative well-differentiated tumour is T2N0 (stage IIA); about 70% 5-year survival in the source (higher with modern adjuvant therapy).

1.explanation: Fever, pain and swelling in a breast-feeding mother is lactational infection progressing to abscess (S. aureus): ultrasound-guided aspiration plus flucloxacillin.

2.explanation: Fine linear branching microcalcification suggests DCIS; vacuum-assisted (stereotactic) biopsy samples calcifications more reliably than standard core biopsy.

3.explanation: A sudden painful discrete lump in a perimenopausal woman is a cyst; ultrasound confirms it and aspiration relieves it.

4.explanation: Bilateral cyclical pain and lumpiness worse before periods is ANDI (fibroadenosis/cyclical mastalgia): reassurance, a supportive bra and simple analgesia.

5.explanation: Several young relatives with breast cancer means genetic counselling and BRCA1/2 testing before planning surveillance or risk-reducing surgery.

6.explanation: A large, rapidly growing mass with stretched shiny skin in a woman over 40 is a phyllodes tumour; treat by wide excision with clear margins.

7.explanation: A hard enlarging lump with a spiculated mammographic mass is cancer until proven otherwise: core needle biopsy gives histology and receptor status.

8.explanation: A painless lump appearing after stopping breast-feeding is a galactocele (milk-retention cyst); aspiration of milky fluid is diagnostic and curative.

9.explanation: Breast enlargement in a pubertal boy is physiological gynaecomastia, which usually settles within 2 years; exclude drugs (e.g. cannabis) and hormonal causes.

10.explanation: Invasive lobular carcinoma is often multifocal and bilateral and underestimated on mammography, so MRI is used to define its extent before surgery.

11.explanation: Bilateral greenish-black multiduct discharge in a postmenopausal woman is duct ectasia; reassure if imaging is normal.

12.explanation: A painless, discrete, very mobile lump in a young woman is a fibroadenoma (‘breast mouse’); confirm with ultrasound and core biopsy.

13.explanation: A painless unilateral subareolar lump in a middle-aged man is male breast cancer until proven otherwise; gynaecomastia is usually bilateral, soft and tender.

1.explanation: A hard, irregular lump with axillary nodes in an elderly woman is breast carcinoma; confirm by triple assessment.

2.explanation: Nipple retraction with green-yellow discharge and dilated ducts on ultrasound is duct ectasia.

3.explanation: A smooth, highly mobile lump in a 21-year-old with benign cytology (C2) is a fibroadenoma.

4.explanation: A non-itchy eczema-like rash of the nipple and areola with an underlying mass is Paget disease of the nipple, usually with underlying carcinoma.

5.explanation: A tender, inflamed breast with fever 2 weeks postpartum and no mass is lactational mastitis; continue breast-feeding and give flucloxacillin.

1.explanation: A 92-year-old with ER-positive disease is treated with primary endocrine therapy (tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor) rather than surgery.

2.explanation: DCIS throughout all quadrants cannot be excised with conservation: mastectomy, with immediate reconstruction in a young woman.

3.explanation: A 2-cm ER-positive cancer with a clinically negative axilla: wide local excision and sentinel node biopsy, then radiotherapy and endocrine therapy.

5.explanation: A firm lump with skin dimpling (tethering) in a 72-year-old is breast cancer; peau d’orange is skin oedema from lymphatic blockage, not a diagnosis.

24-h pH monitoring is the most accurate test for GORD; staging laparoscopy, manometry (motility disorders) and Raman spectroscopy all have roles. OGD, not barium, is first-line for heartburn.

set.stem: A patient has a symptomatic pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum). What is the most important aspect of treatment?
options: elevation of the head of the bed
set.explanation: Cricopharyngeal muscle myotomy Myotomy is key to relieve the underlying neuromotor dysfunction.

options: double dose proton-pump inhibitor and repeat endoscopy in 3 months
proton-pump inhibitor and H₂ blocker, followed by repeat endoscopy in 3 months
antibiotic treatment for Helicobacter pylori with proton-pump inhibitor
Endoscopic resection and ablation (oesophagectomy if endoscopic therapy is not possible)
set.explanation: Barrett oesophagus with high-grade dysplasia is now treated by endoscopic eradication (EMR of visible lesions plus radiofrequency ablation); oesophagectomy is reserved for failures or invasive disease.
The cervical oesophagus is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery, the thoracic part by aortic branches and the abdominal part by the left gastric artery.
Low-grade dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus: high-dose PPI and repeat endoscopy at 6 months; confirmed persistent LGD is then offered radiofrequency ablation.
New reflux symptoms in a 72-year-old need OGD first, to see the mucosa, take biopsies and exclude malignancy; pH studies come later if the diagnosis is unclear.
Young dyspeptic patients without alarm features are managed by ‘test and treat’: confirm H. pylori (urea breath or stool antigen test) before giving eradication therapy.

set.stem: OGD biopsy in the same patient shows high-grade lymphoid tissue suggestive of gastric MALT lymphoma. Besides chemoradiation, what is the appropriate medical treatment?
set.explanation: Pylori eradication is appropriate when high-grade lymphoid tissue is found, suggesting MALToma.
Eradication therapy should follow a positive test (urea breath or stool antigen); a 59-year-old with persistent symptoms also needs OGD if they do not settle.
A patient with previous ulcer starting an NSAID should be tested and treated for H. pylori and given PPI gastroprotection.
Parietal cells secrete H⁺ via the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase and somatostatin inhibits acid. Histamine acts on parietal cells, the vagus mediates the cephalic phase and secretin inhibits acid.
False: Ménétrier disease causes hypochlorhydria and results from increased (not reduced) TGF-α signalling. It gives giant folds, protein loss and anaemia; gastrectomy is a last resort.
Perforated duodenal ulcer The sudden onset and radiographic pneumoperitoneum in a patient with a history of peptic pain point to a perforated duodenal ulcer.
Fiberoptic upper endoscopy Endoscopy is the most reliable diagnostic tool for gastric ulcers.

Uncomplicated intussusception in a stable child is reduced by image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema (~80% success); surgery is for peritonitis, perforation or failed reduction.
Alvarado: migratory pain 1, anorexia 1, nausea/vomiting 1, fever 1; no RIF tenderness, rebound, leucocytosis or left shift = 4 (low probability; pyuria suggests UTI).

set.stem: A 37-year-old diabetic woman has had severe loose motions for 24 hours with vague left-sided abdominal pain and tenesmus; the last motion contained blood. There is mild lower abdominal tenderness; pulse 103/min, BP 121/82 mmHg, temperature 37.3 °C; WBC 12 000/mm³, HbA1c 7.8%. Ultrasound shows small asymptomatic gallstones. What is the most likely diagnosis and the first investigation?

set.explanation: Generalised peritonitis from perforated diverticulitis needs sigmoid resection: primary anastomosis (± defunctioning ileostomy) if stable, Hartmann procedure if unstable or faecal contamination.
Swinging fever, hiccups, right shoulder-tip pain and RUQ tenderness days after repair of a perforated ulcer is a right subhepatic/subphrenic abscess: CT, then percutaneous drainage.
Mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips with hamartomatous GI polyps is Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, which is not listed; polyps cause bleeding and intussusception.
Sudden peritonitis with free gas in the 2nd–3rd week of typhoid fever is perforation of a Peyer patch ulcer in the terminal ileum; resuscitate and operate.
Left iliac fossa pain with dark-red rectal bleeding in a constipated, overweight older woman suggests diverticular disease; colorectal cancer must still be excluded by colonoscopy.
In children, right lower lobe (basal) pneumonia commonly mimics appendicitis through referred pain from the T10–T12 nerves; examine the chest and get a CXR.
Acute severe UC with fever, tachycardia and colonic dilatation needs admission, IV hydrocortisone and daily review; no response in 3–5 days means rescue therapy or colectomy.
Iron-deficiency anaemia, occult blood and a right iliac fossa mass in a 60-year-old is caecal carcinoma until proven otherwise: colonoscopy and CT.
Urinary retention is the commonest early complication of haemorrhoidectomy (pain, spinal anaesthesia, excess fluid); bleeding is the other early concern.
Appendiceal adenocarcinoma with lymphatic invasion needs a right hemicolectomy for nodal clearance; adjuvant chemotherapy depends on nodal stage. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not standard.
Approximately 25% of the global population – especially in poor sanitation settings – are affected.
Eggs passed in stool hatch in the gut; larvae migrate via portal blood and liver to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed, then mature in the intestine.
The small bowel digests and absorbs, the colon mainly absorbs water and ~1 L of ileal content enters the colon daily. B12 and bile salts are absorbed in the terminal ileum.
UC begins in the rectum and spreads proximally, is mucosal (not transmural) and lacks granulomas (a Crohn feature); toxic megacolon typically dilates the transverse colon.
An ileoanal pouch needs a normal sphincter and is for UC/FAP, not Crohn disease; pouch failure ~15%, obstruction 10–15% and pouchitis ~30%.
Meckel diverticulum may bleed (ectopic gastric mucosa) and causes periumbilical pain; it is best shown by a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, not barium.
False: colonic diverticula are pulsion (false) diverticula of mucosa and submucosa only, herniating where vessels pierce the muscle.
Thrombosis occurs at the SMA origin; pain out of proportion to signs is the hallmark. Ischaemic colitis favours the splenic flexure and may stricture; angiodysplasia is right-sided.

Diverticulitis The clinical picture and CT findings are most consistent with diverticulitis.

Intussusception The infant’s intermittent colicky pain and currant jelly stool are typical for intussusception.

options: IV fluid rehydration and a hydrostatic barium enema
IV fluid rehydration, NG decompression, and a UGI contrast study
set.explanation: After IV rehydration, intussusception is reduced by an image-guided enema (air/pneumatic now preferred to barium); surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.
Midgut volvulus The clinical and radiographic findings are most consistent with midgut volvulus.
Duodenal atresia The classic double bubble in a Down syndrome infant is diagnostic for duodenal atresia.
Admit, rehydrate and stop the causative antibiotic; oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is now first-line for C. difficile, metronidazole only where these are unavailable.
In Africa, Asia and South America sigmoid volvulus is the commonest cause of large-bowel obstruction; in the West it is colorectal cancer. Hernias mainly obstruct the small bowel.

set.explanation: First-line treatment of uncomplicated intussusception is image-guided air (pneumatic) or contrast enema reduction; surgery if it fails or there is peritonitis.
CT with contrast is the investigation of choice for a suspected diverticular abscess and guides percutaneous drainage.
Diarrhoea with fever after a recent admission and antibiotics suggests C. difficile colitis; of these options, oral metronidazole (oral vancomycin is now first-line).
A stable infant with intussusception (colic, ‘red-currant jelly’ stool) is treated first by image-guided air/contrast enema reduction.
Six weeks of bloody mucoid diarrhoea with urgency in a young man is ulcerative colitis until proven otherwise: stool cultures, then colonoscopy with biopsies.
Acute LIF pain, fever and raised WCC/CRP in a 65-year-old is acute sigmoid diverticulitis; confirm with CT if severe or uncertain.
Swinging fever with a pericolic abscess on CT in a stable patient without peritonitis: CT-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics.
Abdominal pain, fever and tachycardia on day 5 after colectomy is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise: start IV antibiotics with resuscitation, then CT or re-laparotomy.
The jejunum is thicker walled, redder, with prominent plicae and less lymphoid tissue, and secretes most digestive fluid; the ileum is thinner, paler, with Peyer patches.
Before appendicectomy in a girl of reproductive age, a pregnancy test is mandatory; other imaging rarely changes a clear clinical decision.
Intermittent inconsolable distress, vomiting and ‘red-currant jelly’ stools in an infant is ileocolic intussusception; ultrasound shows a target sign.

set.stem: A 37-year-old man with a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis has a sessile polyp with high-grade dysplasia 10 cm from the anal verge. Which operation is most appropriate?
set.explanation: High-grade dysplasia in UC marks a field change: total proctocolectomy, with an ileoanal J-pouch to preserve continence.

set.stem: A 33-year-old man with Crohn disease has severe abdominal pain and fever: HR 130/min, BP 105/62 mmHg, temperature 38.9 °C, WCC 32 000/mm³; plain films show a markedly dilated colon. Which operation is most appropriate?
set.explanation: Toxic megacolon failing medical therapy is treated by subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy, leaving the rectum for later reconstruction.
Adhesions are the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction in the West, followed by hernias and malignancy.
Symptomatic Meckel diverticulum (bleeding, obstruction from intussusception or volvulus, diverticulitis or perforation) needs resection.
Severe unilateral lower abdominal pain in a young woman with normal inflammatory markers and negative β-hCG suggests an ovarian cyst (rupture or torsion); pelvic ultrasound.

set.explanation: A large cylindrical prolapse on straining in an 84-year-old is full-thickness rectal prolapse; start with stool softeners and bowel-habit advice, then Delorme or rectopexy if needed.
A fluctuant natal-cleft swelling with midline pits is a pilonidal abscess: incision and drainage (off the midline); definitive excision later once the sepsis settles.
An acute perianal abscess over a known fistula needs examination under anaesthesia with incision and drainage (and laying open or seton of any fistula found).
A posterior midline fissure is treated first with topical diltiazem (or GTN) plus stool softeners; botulinum toxin or lateral sphincterotomy if it fails.
Melaena, epigastric pain, weight loss and a Virchow node suggest gastric cancer: OGD with biopsy is needed for tissue diagnosis, then CT for staging.
Coffee-ground vomiting is upper GI bleeding: OGD (within 24 h, sooner if unstable) to find and treat the source.
Haematemesis with jaundice and ascites in an alcoholic suggests portal hypertension and bleeding oesophageal varices.

set.stem: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after fainting at home. He has passed bright red blood per rectum for 6 hours, without abdominal pain or vomiting. Pulse 110/min, BP 95/50 mmHg; there is gross blood on rectal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Sudden painless massive bright-red rectal bleeding in an older patient is most often diverticular.

set.stem: A 56-year-old woman had an episode of melaena 48 hours ago that has not recurred. She had an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 2 years ago. Upper GI endoscopy to the duodenal bulb and colonoscopy are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A ‘herald’ GI bleed after aortic graft surgery is an aortoenteric fistula (usually 3rd/4th part of duodenum) until proven otherwise: CT angiography.

set.stem: A 65-year-old woman has severe fatigue and weakness. She has hypertension, diabetes and coronary disease, takes daily aspirin and has a 40 pack-year smoking history. She is pale, her stool is positive for occult blood and she has a microcytic anaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Occult bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia in an older patient is colorectal (often right-sided) cancer until proven otherwise: colonoscopy.

set.stem: A 65-year-old man has haematemesis and melaena. He has had abdominal pain for 3–4 weeks and has taken ibuprofen four times daily for 3 weeks, with alcohol, for the pain. Pulse 100/min, BP 100/60 mmHg after resuscitation; there is RUQ and epigastric tenderness and melaena on rectal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Regular NSAIDs and alcohol cause gastric mucosal ulceration; a bleeding gastric ulcer is most likely.

set.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic alcoholism has an episode of haematemesis. Pulse 120/min, BP 90/60 mmHg; there are spider naevi, palmar erythema and a distended, non-tender abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Stigmata of chronic liver disease with haematemesis and shock point to bleeding oesophageal varices.

set.stem: A 35-year-old man has haematemesis and black tarry stools after 2 weeks of epigastric pain partly relieved by antacids. Pulse 110/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, with epigastric tenderness and melaena. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Epigastric pain relieved by antacids followed by haematemesis and melaena is a bleeding peptic (usually duodenal) ulcer.

set.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a 1-week history of bloody diarrhoea, 1 month of abdominal pain and 10 lb weight loss. Temperature 38.3 °C, pulse 85/min, BP 110/60 mmHg; the abdomen is diffusely tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea with fever and weight loss in a young adult suggests ulcerative colitis.
Bloody diarrhoea days after AAA repair is ischaemic colitis from IMA ligation; confirm by sigmoidoscopy.
New constipation with narrow stools and dark-red bleeding in an elderly woman is left-sided colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.
Massive lower GI bleeding with shock and no source on examination: after resuscitation (and OGD if upper source possible), CT/mesenteric angiography localises and allows embolisation.
Years of bright-red blood on the paper without bowel change suggests haemorrhoids: proctoscopy/rigid sigmoidoscopy in clinic first; colonoscopy if red flags.
Profuse rectal bleeding with shock: resuscitation comes first — two large-bore cannulae, bloods, cross-match and fluids/blood — before investigations.

Screening aims at detecting disease in an asymptomatic stage
Accurate diagnosis is the key to successful management

set.explanation: A malignant pedunculated polyp confined to the head (Haggitt 1–2) with a clear margin (>1–2 mm), well differentiated and no lymphovascular invasion is cured by polypectomy: surveillance.

A tumour 2 cm from the anal margin involves the sphincter complex, so abdominoperineal resection with permanent colostomy is needed (after neoadjuvant therapy as indicated).

A colonic carcinoma on colonoscopy is staged with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for liver and lung metastases before planning resection.
Adenocarcinoma, arising in Barrett mucosa, is now the commonest oesophageal cancer in the West and typically lies in the distal oesophagus.
Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with blood group A, H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, smoking and nitrosamine-rich diets.

set.stem: A 35-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was thrown against the steering column, sustaining blunt trauma to his left upper abdomen. On arrival at the emergency department he complains of abdominal pain but is haemodynamically stable. CT shows a splenic tear with a small intra-abdominal haematoma; the tear extends through the splenic capsule but not to the hilum. Which one of the following treatment options is least likely to be indicated at this time?
options: Serial haemoglobin measurement and abdominal examination.
set.explanation: A haemodynamically stable patient with a non-hilar splenic laceration is managed non-operatively (HDU monitoring, cross-match, serial examination/imaging); laparotomy is for instability or peritonitis.

Abdominal discoloration at specific sites denotes underlying serious pathology.
Free movement of the abdominal wall on respiration makes generalised peritonitis unlikely.
Rebound tenderness is best tested by gentle percussion.
An intra-abdominal lump becomes prominent when the patient tenses the abdomen or lifts the head from the bed.
set.explanation: False: E — an intra-abdominal lump becomes less prominent when the abdominal muscles are tensed (head-raising test); a lump in the abdominal wall stays palpable.

Placement of a central venous line

set.stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after sustaining a single gunshot wound to the right chest. He is awake and alert and complaining of significant abdominal pain and chest pain. He has a pulse of 110, blood pressure (BP) of 90/60, respirations of 24. On examination, his breath sounds are decreased on the right. His chest is dull to percussion on the right. His abdomen is slightly distended and diffusely tender. His pulse oximeter shows 88% on 6 L oxygen by face mask. A right chest drain is inserted and he responds to resuscitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: A gunshot wound to the lower chest with abdominal distension and tenderness implies transdiaphragmatic injury and mandates laparotomy once the haemothorax is drained.

set.stem: Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for suspected spontaneous oesophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome)?
set.explanation: A water-soluble contrast oesophagogram is the classic test to confirm and localise the leak; CT with oral contrast is used if it is equivocal or the patient is unwell.

set.stem: Which is the treatment of choice for a post-traumatic duodenal haematoma causing obstruction?
set.explanation: Most duodenal haematomas resolve within 2–3 weeks with NG decompression and parenteral nutrition; surgery only if obstruction persists or perforation is suspected.

Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is contraindicated in the presence of an indication for explorative laparotomy

Increasing lower abdominal pain with sudden worsening, guarding, tachycardia and poor capillary refill in a young woman is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until a pregnancy test excludes it.

set.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to the ER following an automobile accident in which his chest struck the steering wheel. His vital signs are heart rate of 78 beats/minute, blood pressure of 129/65, respirations of 14 breaths/minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Examination reveals no evidence of respiratory distress, but the patient exhibits multiple right-sided palpable rib fractures. A right-sided chest wall segment appears to move inward rather than outward during inspiration and outward rather than inward during expiration. Chest x-ray shows no evidence of pneumothorax or hemothorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
set.explanation: Flail chest without respiratory compromise is managed with good analgesia (e.g. epidural or regional block) and physiotherapy; ventilation only if respiratory failure develops.
A gunshot wound below the nipple line may cross the diaphragm and needs laparotomy; thoracotomy is reserved for massive or persistent chest drain output.
Hypotension after trauma is haemorrhage until proven otherwise, not head injury; FAST rapidly identifies abdominal bleeding in the unstable patient.

A normotensive pregnant patient with a positive FAST needs CT abdomen/pelvis; maternal stabilisation and diagnosis take priority over fetal radiation risk.
A haemodynamically stable patient with splenic injury and no contrast extravasation is managed non-operatively with observation; angioembolisation if there is a blush.

set.stem: A patient with a hydatid liver cyst is scheduled for surgery. Is there a benefit of giving medication before surgery? Why?
options: No, medications before surgery have no impact
Yes, albendazole (± praziquantel) inactivates the cyst and lowers intracystic pressure, reducing the risk of recurrence
No, they only increase the risk of infection
Yes, they are used to anesthetize the patient
set.explanation: Preoperative albendazole (± praziquantel) kills protoscolices and softens the cyst, reducing the risk of secondary hydatidosis and recurrence if spillage occurs.

set.stem: A jaundiced patient has a hydatid liver cyst with daughter cysts on CT and is planned for surgery. What further imaging would you order before surgery?
set.explanation: Jaundice suggests cyst–biliary communication; MRCP shows the biliary tree and any communication before surgery. Ultrasound is first-line but adds little after CT.

set.stem: After surgery for a hydatid liver cyst, what is your plan for minimising the risk of recurrence or reinfection?
options: Use prophylactic antibiotics only during surgery
Continue albendazole (± praziquantel) postoperatively and educate the patient about hand hygiene, clean food and water and avoiding contact with dogs
set.explanation: Postoperative albendazole (usually 1–3 months) kills any spilled protoscolices, and hygiene education (dogs, unwashed vegetables) prevents reinfection.

set.stem: A patient with right upper quadrant pain has the imaging shown. What is the imaging modality and what does it show?
options: CT scan showing a cystic liver lesion with floating detached membranes (water-lily sign)
set.explanation: Contrast CT shows a liver cyst with detached, floating endocyst membranes (water-lily sign), diagnostic of a hydatid cyst.

set.stem: What is the usual surgical option for an uncomplicated hydatid liver cyst?
set.explanation: Conservative surgery (cyst evacuation with partial cystectomy or pericystectomy under scolicidal cover) is standard; formal hepatectomy is reserved for selected cases.

set.stem: A patient with upper abdominal pain did not respond to H. pylori eradication therapy, and an ultrasound reveals a 4.5 × 3 cm cyst in the liver. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A cystic liver lesion may be a simple cyst, an abscess or a hydatid (Echinococcus granulosus) cyst; haemangioma, FNH, HCC and metastases are usually solid.

options: Liver biopsy to confirm the diagnosis

set.explanation: Ultrasound stages the cyst (WHO-IWGE classification: active, transitional or inactive), which decides between drugs, PAIR, surgery or watch-and-wait.

set.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with fevers and right upper abdominal pain following a 1-week history of bloody diarrhoea. He has recently returned from holiday in the Maldives, but has previously been fit and well. On examination, he has a tender palpable liver. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
set.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea after travel followed by fever and a tender liver suggests amoebic liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica colitis.
Confusion (encephalopathy), jaundice, ascites and caput medusae indicate decompensated cirrhosis, most commonly due to alcohol in the UK.

set.stem: Four weeks after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a patient's abdominal drain is still draining 900 mL of bile daily. What is the best minimally invasive treatment?
options: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stent placement
set.explanation: ERCP with sphincterotomy and stenting removes the sphincter pressure gradient so bile drains into the duodenum, allowing a cystic stump leak to seal.

set.stem: A diabetic woman has small gallstones found incidentally on ultrasound. She has never had biliary pain. Is surgery needed for her gallbladder?
options: No, surgery is not indicated because she is asymptomatic regarding gallstones.
Yes, as she is diabetic (indication in asymptomatic gallstone disease).
No, because the gallstones are small and less than 7mm.
Yes, because any gallstones in diabetic patients always require cholecystectomy.
Yes, because all gallstones should be removed once detected
set.explanation: Asymptomatic gallstones do not need cholecystectomy (NICE), and diabetes is no longer considered an indication; surgery is offered once symptoms develop.

set.stem: A 51-year-old male smoker presents with upper abdominal discomfort and heaviness over the past few weeks, along with a substernal burning sensation. set.explanation: Ursodeoxycholic acid lowers biliary cholesterol saturation and can dissolve small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder; recurrence is common.

set.stem: A patient with gallstones who declined cholecystectomy develops itching two years later. The imaging shown is performed. What is the study and what are the findings?

set.explanation: Symptomatic CBD stones are cleared by ERCP with sphincterotomy and extraction, followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence.

set.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with 6 months of epigastric discomfort, poor appetite and weight loss. Abdominal ultrasound reveals cholelithiasis, and an upper GI contrast series is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: The barium study shows a gastric ulcer; with weight loss it needs endoscopic biopsy to exclude malignancy. The gallstones are incidental.

options: Radioisotope scanning with preimaging phenobarbital administration
set.explanation: Phenobarbital priming enhances hepatic excretion, so absent bowel excretion on HIDA scanning is highly sensitive for biliary atresia.
Sudden cardiorespiratory collapse during laparoscopy (raised IAP, capnothorax, CO2 embolism) is first managed by releasing the pneumoperitoneum, then reassessing.

set.stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted with severe epigastric pain and vomiting. The pain is continuous and worse on movement. On examination she is lying still, taking shallow breaths and sweating. There is marked tenderness in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, Murphy's sign is positive and she is slightly pyrexial. You suspect acute cholecystitis. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
set.explanation: Suspected acute cholecystitis is managed first with nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics; ultrasound then confirms it before early cholecystectomy.

set.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with an acute episode of epigastric pain, vomiting and fever. The registrar, who has already clerked and examined the patient, tells you that Murphy's sign is positive. Without having seen the patient, what is the most likely diagnosis?

You are asked to see a 48-year-old woman admitted with sudden onset of right upper quadrant pain. Your registrar, having seen her, tells you that the patient has Charcot's triad. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 44-year-old woman presents with acute onset of right upper quadrant pain and fever. On examination, she is lying still and has a tachycardia. The abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant with guarding in that area. Murphy's sign is positive. What is the most useful investigation for this patient?

set.explanation: Absent urinary urobilinogen means conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the gut, i.e. biliary obstruction such as a CBD stone; haemolysis and Gilbert give unconjugated jaundice.

set.stem: A 23-year-old woman undergoes a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent biliary colic. On examination of the gallbladder there are stones present (see figure). Which is the single most likely underlying diagnosis to explain her condition?

A 47-year-old man has had malaise and anorexia for 2 weeks and has developed jaundice over 3 days. Serum testing confirms hepatitis A infection. Blood tests are taken to assess the cause of his jaundice (normal ranges are shown). Which is the single most likely combination of blood results in this patient?

A 62-year-old man presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. Blood tests show elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid and a common bile duct of 1.0 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 36-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice. She is febrile and tachycardic. Blood tests show leukocytosis and elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid and a common bile duct of 1.0 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Fever and tachycardia with jaundice, RUQ pain and a dilated CBD (Charcot's triad) indicate acute cholangitis needing antibiotics and biliary drainage.

set.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal pain; each episode lasts 1 to 2 hours. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. White cell count, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, amylase and lipase are normal. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid and a common bile duct of 3 mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

set.explanation: Beyond T1a, gallbladder cancer needs radical cholecystectomy: en bloc resection of liver segments IVb/V with portal lymphadenectomy; simple cholecystectomy suffices only for T1a.
Boas sign (hyperaesthesia below the right scapula) is associated with acute cholecystitis; Cullen and Grey Turner signs suggest haemorrhagic pancreatitis.

set.stem: A patient with known gallstones and mild jaundice is rushed into the emergency department with severe diffuse abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. The abdomen is tender with some rigidity in its upper part; bowel sounds are present. Pulse 108/min, BP 105/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Severe upper abdominal pain with rigidity, tachycardia and tachypnoea in a jaundiced patient with gallstones indicates acute biliary pancreatitis from a CBD stone.

set.stem: In this patient with suspected acute pancreatitis, which TWO initial investigations best establish the diagnosis?
set.explanation: Serum lipase or amylase >3 times normal with typical pain makes the diagnosis; CT confirms it when in doubt and later assesses necrosis.

set.stem: How can acute pancreatitis be confirmed radiologically in this patient?
set.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT shows a diffusely enlarged, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic stranding and, after 72 h, any necrosis.

set.stem: What is the treatment of this patient with severe acute biliary pancreatitis?
options: Admission to HDU/ICU with fluid resuscitation and analgesia, then ERCP (for cholangitis or persisting obstruction) and cholecystectomy for definitive treatment
Conservative management with dietary restrictions only
set.explanation: Severe biliary pancreatitis needs monitored resuscitation and analgesia; ERCP for cholangitis/obstruction and cholecystectomy on recovery prevent recurrence.

set.stem: A 33-year-old woman has severe upper abdominal pain with radiation to the back within 24 hours of removing gallstones in the common bile duct by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). The pain is eased when she leans forward. She reports some nausea and vomiting but denies any diarrhoea. Jaundice is noted and the epigastric region is tender on palpation. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and temperature is 37.3°C. What is the SINGLE most likely reason for her signs and symptoms?

options: The vast majority of the acinar tissue is endocrine.
The pancreatic tail snugly fits into the splenic hilum.
The pancreatic digestive enzymes are acidic in nature with a pH of 7.
The islets of Langerhans contain several hormone-producing cell types (alpha, beta, delta and PP cells).
The amount of pancreatic juice secreted is 1200 to 1500 mLs in 24 hours.

set.explanation: A and C are false: amylase is not specific (also raised in perforation, ischaemia) and urinary amylase/clearance ratio is unreliable; lipase is more sensitive and specific.
A is false: pancreatic injury is uncommon in blunt trauma; it usually accompanies liver, spleen or duodenal injury, and CECT and ERCP/MRCP define duct damage.
Amylase may be normal with late presentation, hypertriglyceridaemia or acute-on-chronic disease, and its level does not reflect severity.
A is false: pancreatitis follows about 3–5% of ERCPs (more after therapeutic procedures); cardiac surgery, gastrectomy and retained CBD stones are recognised causes.
Grey Turner's (flank) and Cullen's (periumbilical) bruising occur, and hypocalcaemia may give Trousseau's sign; Courvoisier's and Murphy's signs are biliary.

options: Establish large-bore intravenous access, cross-match blood and begin cautious (permissive hypotensive) resuscitation
Send for a computed tomography scan of the abdomen
Obtain blood to determine haemoglobin and amylase levels
Request an abdominal plain film radiograph
set.explanation: A shocked patient with a pulsatile mass has a ruptured AAA: secure IV access, cross-match and resuscitate to permissive hypotension en route to theatre; CT only if stable.

set.stem: A 50-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back together with nausea and vomiting. Examination reveals localised epigastric peritonitis and investigations reveal an amylase of 650 IU/L. Which of the following would indicate a poor prognosis in this condition?

set.explanation: Painless progressive jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law) suggests carcinoma of the pancreatic head.
One point per Glasgow criterion (age >55, WCC >15, glucose >10, urea >16, PaO2 <8 kPa, Ca <2, albumin <32, LDH >600); this patient meets three.
Raised cyst-fluid CEA indicates a mucinous (premalignant) cystic neoplasm; a symptomatic body/tail lesion in a fit patient is treated by distal pancreatectomy.
Sudden RIF pain on exertion with a tender abdominal wall mass on ultrasound suggests rectus sheath haematoma from inferior epigastric vessel rupture.
Total pancreatectomy removes all endocrine and exocrine tissue, causing brittle diabetes and steatorrhoea needing insulin and enzyme replacement.

set.stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with epigastric abdominal pain and nausea. She is afebrile with normal vital signs. On laboratory results she has no leukocytosis with normal levels of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. The amylase and lipase are elevated. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid, and a common bile duct of 3 mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

set.explanation: Periumbilical bruising (Cullen's sign) reflects retroperitoneal haemorrhage, e.g. haemorrhagic pancreatitis; flank bruising is Grey Turner's sign.
Weight loss with a Virchow node (and a heliotrope rash of paraneoplastic dermatomyositis) suggests gastric cancer; endoscopy with biopsy confirms it.

set.stem: Anatomy of the spleen. Which of the following statements are true?
options: The splenic vessels are contained within the splenorenal ligament.
The splenic artery arises from the left gastric artery.
The short gastric branches of the splenic artery lie within the gastrosplenic ligament.
The spleen is a major site of immune function.
Haemopoiesis occurs in the foetal spleen.
set.explanation: B is false: the splenic artery arises from the coeliac trunk, not the left gastric artery. The other statements are true.
set.notes: The original stem had a separate pancreatic pseudocyst question merged into it (42-year-old, palpable epigastric mass 6 weeks after acute pancreatitis; options stomach cancer / pancreatic cystadenoma / liver edge / pancreatic malignancy / pseudocyst; answer E pseudocyst). That question was removed from this stem and exists nowhere else; re-add it to panc if wanted.

set.stem: Anatomy of the spleen. All of the following statements are true except:
options: The spleen lies in front of the left seventh, eighth, and ninth ribs.
The tail of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament.
The lymphatics of the spleen ultimately drain into the coeliac nodes.
The left extremity of the lesser sac lies against the splenic hilum.
The visceral surface has impressions for the stomach, left kidney and splenic flexure of the colon.
set.explanation: A is false: the spleen lies deep to the left 9th–11th ribs, its long axis along the 10th rib.

options: Platelet transfusion when the count drops below 50 000/µL
Expectant management with intervention only if significant bleeding occurs
set.explanation: ITP with significant bleeding is treated first with corticosteroids (± IVIg); splenectomy is reserved for refractory or relapsing disease.

set.stem: A patient with ITP initially responds to steroids, but over 6–12 months the responses become less marked and shorter, with increasing side effects. What is the next step in management?
options: Increase in steroid dose and frequency
set.explanation: Steroid-dependent ITP with waning responses and rising side effects is an indication for splenectomy, which gives durable remission in about two-thirds.
Bite cells occur in oxidative haemolysis (e.g. G6PD deficiency) as the spleen removes Heinz bodies; Howell–Jolly bodies, target cells and Pappenheimer bodies indicate hyposplenism.
Hypokalaemia causes polyuria and thirst; with high-normal sodium in a young adult this suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), usually with hypertension.

set.stem: A patient with mild skin pigmentation is admitted emergently because of sudden abdominal pain, fever and a rigid abdomen. Her blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. Blood tests show WBC 25 000/µL, glucose 55 mg/dL, sodium 119 mEq/L and potassium 6.2 mEq/L. Exploratory laparotomy shows no intra-abdominal pathology. Which of the following is the definitive treatment for her primary condition?
A 45-year-old woman presents with hypertension, development of facial hair and a 7-cm suprarenal mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A 36-year-old woman presents with palpitations, anxiety and hypertension. Workup reveals a phaeochromocytoma. Which of the following is the best approach to optimising the patient preoperatively?
options: Fluid restriction 24 hours preoperatively to prevent intraoperative congestive heart failure
Initiation of an α-blocker 24 hours prior to surgery
Initiation of an α-blocker at 1 to 3 weeks prior to surgery
Initiation of a β-blocker 1 to 3 weeks prior to surgery
Escalating antihypertensive drug therapy with β-blockade followed by α-blockade starting at least 1 week prior to surgery

set.stem: An obese woman with a strangulated paraumbilical hernia causing small bowel obstruction undergoes emergency surgery, and a segment of gangrenous small bowel is resected. What is the best surgical option for the hernia now, and why?
options: Herniotomy with suture repair (herniorrhaphy); mesh avoided because of the high infection risk in a contaminated field
set.explanation: After resecting gangrenous bowel the field is contaminated, so a sutured repair is preferred; a permanent synthetic mesh carries a high infection risk.

set.stem: An obese middle-aged woman presents with a reducible swelling just above the umbilicus that has slowly enlarged over several months. What is the cause of this mass?
options: Paraumbilical hernia due to obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure
set.explanation: A reducible swelling beside the umbilicus in an obese adult is a paraumbilical hernia through the linea alba, promoted by raised intra-abdominal pressure.

set.stem: Which THREE clinical signs best confirm that this supraumbilical swelling is a paraumbilical hernia?
options: Palpable lump above the umbilicus, reducibility and an expansile cough impulse
set.explanation: A hernia is a lump that reduces and has an expansile cough impulse; redness and tenderness suggest strangulation rather than confirm a hernia.

set.stem: The same woman later develops bilious vomiting and central colicky abdominal pain with distension; the hernia is now tense, tender and irreducible. Her X-ray is shown. What is the study, what does it show, and what is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Dilated central small-bowel loops with air–fluid levels on an erect abdominal film, with a tender irreducible hernia, indicate obstruction from a strangulated paraumbilical hernia.
Moderate hypothyroidism raises anaesthetic risk (hypothermia, hypotension, slow recovery), so elective surgery is postponed until euthyroid.
A femoral hernia (femoral triangle lump in an elderly woman) has a high strangulation risk through its narrow neck, so prompt repair is advised.
A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle may be a femoral hernia, saphena varix or node; a Spigelian hernia lies far higher, at the lateral rectus border.
C and D are false: a hernia (e.g. femoral, obturator) can easily be missed, and an inebriated patient may still have serious surgical pathology.
B and C are false: inguinal hernia remains the commonest hernia in women, and a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
A and B are false: mesh is standard but not mandatory (e.g. Shouldice in selected cases), and Lichtenstein does not have the lowest recurrence of all repairs.
A, B and D are false: mesh may be used selectively in contaminated fields, it acts as a scaffold for tissue ingrowth, and plain polypropylene causes intraperitoneal adhesions.
A, C and E are false: laparoscopic repair is used, femoral hernia risk rises after open inguinal repair, and the femoral vein (not nerve) is at risk.

options: Incisional hernias never develop more than 2 years after the original surgery.
Jenkins Rule states that in closing an abdominal incision the length of suture used should be four times the length of the incision. However, this has been disproved.
Transverse abdominal incisions are less likely to herniate than vertical incisions.
Non-absorbable meshes placed at initial surgery will reduce the risk of subsequent incisional herniation.
Laparoscopic mesh repair of incisional hernia has a lower wound infection rate than open mesh repair.
set.explanation: A and B are false: incisional hernias can appear many years later, and Jenkins' 4:1 suture-length rule remains valid (now with small bites).
Acute pain and vomiting in an elderly patient with a hiatus hernia suggest an obstructed or volvulised paraoesophageal (rolling) hernia; sliding hernias rarely obstruct.

options: Laparotomy or laparoscopy and operative repair
Continued NG tube decompression and total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
Thoracotomy or thoracoscopy and operative repair
set.explanation: An obstructed paraoesophageal hernia risks strangulation and needs prompt (usually laparoscopic) reduction, sac excision and crural repair after decompression.
A tender bulge below the inguinal ligament in an elderly woman with coughing (pneumonia) is an incarcerated femoral hernia.
An intermittent, reducible inguinal bulge in an infant is an indirect inguinal hernia through a patent processus vaginalis.

options: Reassurance that the abnormality will resolve without intervention
Referral to the ED for immediate surgical consultation
set.explanation: Infant inguinal hernias do not resolve and carry a high incarceration risk, so prompt elective herniotomy is arranged.

options: Sedation with manual reduction and arrangements for elective surgical repair
Sedation with manual reduction, admission, rehydration, and surgical repair within 24–48 hours
set.explanation: An incarcerated infant hernia without peritonitis is reduced under sedation, then repaired within 24–48 h once oedema settles, as re-incarceration is common.
Necrotic bowel in the sac means its blood supply has been cut off: a strangulated hernia. Irreducible or obstructed hernias have viable contents.
A tense, tender, red, irreducible hernia with obstruction is strangulated: resuscitate and operate urgently; do not attempt reduction or delay for imaging.
Maydl's hernia has two loops (W) in the sac; the intervening intra-abdominal loop may strangulate unseen, so it must be checked at surgery.

set.stem: A 67-year-old male has a swelling in the right groin that appears and disappears. It lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle and protrudes on coughing. It reappears despite pressure over the deep inguinal ring. What hernia is this most likely to be?

set.explanation: A swelling through the umbilical scar present since birth is a persistent congenital umbilical hernia; paraumbilical hernias are acquired, beside the umbilicus.

2.explanation: Recurrent faints from fasting hypoglycaemia, with obesity from frequent eating and a small pancreatic mass, suggest an insulinoma.

3.explanation: Diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhoea form the inhibitory triad of a somatostatinoma, usually in the pancreatic head.

5.explanation: Refractory duodenal ulceration with a duodenal wall mass in the gastrinoma triangle indicates a gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

2.stem: A 58-year-old man complains of malaise, bilateral backache, nausea and occasional vomiting for 2 months. Clinically there is nothing significant except for bilateral hydroceles, of which the patient was not aware. Routine blood tests reveal: Hb 10 g/dL, ESR 88, CRP 292, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 256 µmol/L, K 6.1 mmol/L, Na 135 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L and HCO₃ 18 mmol/L.

1.explanation: Collapse with an expansile, pulsatile mass above the umbilicus is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise.

2.explanation: Dyspepsia, weight loss, an epigastric mass and a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node indicate gastric carcinoma.

3.explanation: Iron-deficiency (microcytic) anaemia with a right iliac fossa mass in an elderly patient is caecal carcinoma.

4.explanation: Menorrhagia with a knobbly mass arising from the pelvis indicates uterine fibroids (leiomyomas).

5.explanation: A thick-walled fluid collection next to the pancreas in an alcoholic with pancreatitis is a pseudocyst.

2.explanation: Fever, sore throat, posterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae and a rash after ampicillin indicate EBV infectious mononucleosis.

3.explanation: Periodic fever, anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly after travel to India suggest malaria.

4.explanation: Tender hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and jaundice with recurrent miscarriage (antiphospholipid syndrome) suggest Budd–Chiari hepatic vein thrombosis.

5.explanation: Gallstones, anaemia, splenomegaly and spherocytes with a negative direct Coombs test indicate hereditary spherocytosis.

1.explanation: Fasting/exercise-induced faintness and sweating relieved by eating (Whipple's triad) suggests an insulinoma.

2.explanation: Profuse watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and dehydration despite negative stool cultures suggests a VIPoma.

3.explanation: Diabetes, weight loss and necrolytic migratory erythema (blistering rash) indicate a glucagonoma.

5.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a long history of foul-smelling, bulky stools that are becoming more frequent and severe. She also reports increased thirst and passing large amounts of dilute urine. On examination, she appears thin and wasted but there is no other abnormality.
5.explanation: Steatorrhoea plus diabetes (thirst, polyuria) and weight loss form the inhibitory syndrome of a somatostatinoma.

1.stem: A 12-year-old boy undergoing open excision of an appendix mass secondary to acute appendicitis through an oblique muscle-splitting incision centred on McBurney's point.
1.explanation: The gridiron is an oblique muscle-splitting incision through McBurney's point; the Lanz is a more transverse skin-crease version.

1.explanation: Epigastric/right-sided pain for 48 h with fever, tachycardia and leucocytosis but no jaundice indicates acute cholecystitis.

2.explanation: Sudden severe pain radiating to the flank and back with faintness in an elderly man is a leaking AAA until proven otherwise; renal colic does not cause collapse.

3.explanation: Three days of LIF pain with low-grade fever suggests sigmoid diverticulitis; adjacent bladder inflammation explains dysuria and urinary blood/protein.

set.stem: Regarding preliminary investigations of the urinary tract, the following statements are true except:
Regarding urinary tract infection, the following statements are true except:
set.explanation: C is false: urease-producing Proteus and staphylococci make and thrive in alkaline urine. E is false: UTI often presents acutely, e.g. as pyelonephritis or septicaemia.

set.stem: Regarding upper urinary tract infection, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: All are true: sterile pyuria suggests renal TB, pyonephrosis usually follows stone obstruction and a retrocaecal appendix abscess can track to the perinephric space.

set.stem: Regarding urinary fistulae, which of the following statements is not true?
set.explanation: Catheter drainage heals only a minority of small, early post-hysterectomy vesicovaginal fistulae; most need formal vaginal or abdominal repair.

set.stem: Regarding UTI and cystitis, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: D is false: tuberculous cystitis is almost always secondary to renal TB, spreading down the ureter (descending infection), not by haematogenous or lymphatic routes.

set.stem: Regarding inflammation of the urethra, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: A is false: meatal ulcer is typically seen in circumcised infants (ammoniacal dermatitis from wet napkins), not as an STD in middle-aged men.

set.stem: Regarding epididymo-orchitis, which of the following statements are true?

set.explanation: Gonorrhoeae is a glucose-fermenting Gram-negative diplococcus.
Coli is the most common cause of uncomplicated UTIs in young women.
Ketonuria in a febrile type 1 diabetic suggests developing ketoacidosis, so check blood glucose (and ketones) first; imaging follows.
Gram-negative bacteraemia from a urinary source is urosepsis and needs prompt IV antibiotics (with fluids), not oral therapy.
Frequency, dysuria and haematuria with suprapubic tenderness but no fever or loin pain indicate lower urinary tract infection (acute cystitis).
For a renal pelvic stone under 2 cm, ESWL (or flexible ureteroscopy) is first line; PCNL is for stones over 2 cm, and tamsulosin helps only distal ureteric stones.
An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: antibiotics plus urgent decompression (ureteric stent or nephrostomy); definitive stone treatment is delayed.

set.stem: Regarding pain of urological origin, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: E is false: large, slow-growing space-occupying lesions (e.g. hydronephrosis, renal tumours) are often painless or cause only vague discomfort.

set.stem: Regarding imaging in urological conditions, which of the following statements are true?
Regarding urological imaging, the following statements are true except:
set.explanation: B is false: tumour extension into the IVC is assessed by CT or MRI; venography is now obsolete.

set.stem: Regarding renal calculi, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: D is false: pure uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (visible on CT); staghorn calculi are usually struvite from urease-producing infection.

set.stem: Regarding renal and ureteric calculi, which of the following statements are false?

set.explanation: All are used: non-contrast CT KUB is now the investigation of choice; KUB, US and IVU still have roles, and retrograde pyelography is used in selected cases.

set.stem: Regarding management of urinary calculi, the following statements are true except:
set.explanation: A is false: stones under 5 mm usually pass but many 5–10 mm stones do not. D is false: with bilateral stones the better-functioning kidney is usually treated first.
C is false: stones lodge at several narrowings (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ). D is false: most pass, the rest mainly by laser ureteroscopy/ESWL. E is false: pain may settle despite obstruction.

set.stem: Regarding bladder stones, which of the following statements are true?
set.explanation: D is false: most bladder stones are fragmented endoscopically, but large or hard stones may need percutaneous or open cystolithotomy.
Calcium oxalate (alone or mixed with calcium phosphate) forms most urinary stones (about 75–80%), and these are radio-opaque.

set.stem: A 30-year-old PhD student has acute colicky left loin pain suggestive of a urinary calculus. Which initial investigation should he have?
set.explanation: Of these options, a plain KUB film is the initial test (about 90% of stones are radio-opaque); non-contrast CT KUB is now the definitive investigation.
Gout (hyperuricosuria and persistently acidic urine) predisposes to uric acid stones, which are radiolucent on plain film but seen on CT.

set.stem: A 49-year-old postmenopausal woman is admitted following severe attacks of abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. The pain is colicky in nature, starting from the left flank and radiating to the left groin. You are unable to obtain a history as she is writhing in pain. On examination, she is sweating profusely. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 49-year-old woman has severe colicky left flank pain radiating to the left groin, with nausea and vomiting; renal colic is suspected. Which investigation will be of most diagnostic value?
set.explanation: Non-contrast (low-dose) CT KUB is the gold standard for diagnosing urinary stones, showing size and site and excluding other causes such as an aortic aneurysm.
Loin-to-groin colic with haematuria suggests a ureteric stone; non-contrast CT KUB is the first-line imaging test (sensitivity about 97%).
Uric acid stones (gout, tumour lysis after chemotherapy) are prevented by urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate, plus hydration and allopurinol.
Living donors need adequate renal reserve; a GFR of 40 mL/min/1.73 m² excludes donation, whereas BMI 28, single-drug-controlled hypertension and group O are acceptable.
A solid enhancing parenchymal renal mass in an adult is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise; TCC arises from the collecting system and AML contains fat.

options: It is a tumour of embryonic nephrogenic tissue occurring below the age of 5 years.
Haematuria and fever are the most common presentations.
Haematogenous spread is mainly to the lungs.
Imaging modalities are US, CT and MRI.
Treatment is by chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy.

set.stem: Which of the following statements about hypernephroma (renal cell carcinoma) are true?
options: In 25% of patients there are no local symptoms.
A left-sided varicocele might be a presenting feature in a male.
Haematuria and clot colic are the most common presentations.
US and contrast-enhanced CT are the imaging methods of choice.
Following nephrectomy, chemotherapy and radiotherapy should be given.
set.explanation: E is false: renal cell carcinoma is resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so these are not given after nephrectomy; a left varicocele may signal renal vein involvement.

options: It is an incidental finding in fewer than 10% of patients
Women are more commonly affected than men
Renal cell carcinoma accounts for around 3% of adult cancers
Metastases are poorly visualized by standard imaging techniques

set.explanation: Renal cancer in a blind man suggests von Hippel–Lindau disease (retinal angiomas), so genetic counselling and family screening are indicated.
Loin tenderness with low-grade fever and leucocytosis suggests pyelonephritis or a perinephric collection; renal ultrasound is the first-line test for obstruction or abscess.
Von Hippel–Lindau disease is caused by mutation of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p and predisposes to clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
A loin mass with haematuria suggests a renal tumour; contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen characterises the mass and stages it.
Beta-blockers, thiazides, SSRIs such as fluoxetine and 5α-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride can all cause erectile dysfunction; metformin does not.
Low-volume ejaculate with normal sperm in a man on an α-blocker suggests retrograde ejaculation, confirmed by finding sperm in post-ejaculatory urine.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes a hypotonic bladder with chronic retention and dribbling overflow incontinence, as shown by the large post-void residue.
A non-expanding perirenal haematoma in a stable patient is a low-grade (AAST grade II) renal injury, managed non-operatively with bed rest and monitoring.
Blood at the meatus with pelvic fracture and scrotal haematoma suggests urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram before any catheter; suprapubic catheter if disrupted.
Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture heals with urethral catheter drainage for about 10–14 days; intraperitoneal rupture needs surgical repair.
Blood at the meatus after a pelvic fracture suggests posterior urethral injury; perform retrograde urethrography before any urethral catheter is passed.
Sudden severe testicular pain waking an adolescent is torsion until proven otherwise; urgent urological referral for scrotal exploration (within 6 hours) saves the testis.

set.stem: Regarding renal failure, which of the following statements is false?
options: Anuria is defined as complete absence of urine production.
Oliguria is defined as urinary output of less than 400 mL in 24 hours.
Certain drugs can cause renal failure.
All patients with renal failure will require renal replacement therapy.
Indwelling stents can be used to relieve ureteric obstruction.
